(CNN) -- Christine Beatty, chief of staff for former Detroit Mayor Kwame Kilpatrick, pleaded guilty Monday to charges stemming from their text-messaging sex scandal case and will serve four months in jail, according to the Wayne County prosecutor's office. Under a plea deal, Christine Beatty, shown in August at an arraignment in Detroit, will serve five years probation. Beatty pleaded guilty to two counts of obstruction of justice, according to Maria Miller, the prosecutor's spokeswoman. Charges of perjury and misconduct against Beatty will be dropped as part of the plea arrangement, she said. Beatty agreed to a plea arrangement under which she will serve five years probation -- the first 120 days to be served in jail -- and pay a $100,000 fine, "based on [Beatty's] ability to pay," Miller said. Beatty will begin serving her jail sentence on January 5, when she will be formally sentenced, Miller said. Kym L. Worthy, prosecuting attorney for Wayne County, released a statement saying she is "very pleased that this defendant admitted her guilt." "We live in an age where greed and protecting one's secrets is glorified and accepted," Worthy said. "Now the city of Detroit, the region and the state of Michigan can truly begin to move forward when this ugly chapter in Detroit's history is put to rest." In September, Kilpatrick resigned as mayor and pleaded guilty to two felony obstruction of justice charges stemming from his efforts to cover up his relationship with Beatty. Like Beatty, Kilpatrick was sentenced to five years probation with the first four months to be served in jail. He is serving that sentence in the Wayne County jail. At the time of his sentencing in October, the judge in the case called Kilpatrick "arrogant and defiant," particularly for a televised speech that aired hours after Kilpatrick entered his pleas. "That night, the community expected to hear a message of humility, remorse and apology," Wayne County Circuit Judge David Groner said at Kilpatrick's sentencing. "Instead, we heard an arrogant and defiant man who accused the governor, among others, for his downfall." In addition to his jail and probation sentence, Kilpatrick must also pay the city of Detroit $1 million in restitution, and forfeit any future pension. Initially, Kilpatrick was accused of blocking a criminal investigation into his office and firing a police deputy to cover up an affair with Beatty, then his chief of staff. When that deputy, Gary Brown, filed a whistle-blower suit, Kilpatrick and Beatty denied under oath that an affair had taken place between them. Text messages that contradicted Kilpatrick's and Beatty's denials of an affair were made public in January by the Detroit Free Press, and county prosecutor Worthy charged Kilpatrick and Beatty with multiple counts of perjury, obstruction of justice and misconduct in office. The most serious charges would have carried a maximum penalty of 15 years in prison upon conviction. Beatty resigned her post after the text messages were made public. Kilpatrick initially refused to resign after the scandal broke, and Michigan Gov. Jennifer Granholm called a hearing on whether she should remove him from office at the request of the Detroit City Council. Granholm adjourned those hearings after Kilpatrick pleaded guilty and resigned in September.

**DETROIT — Christine Beatty, the former chief of staff whose intimate text messages with ex-Mayor Kwame Kilpatrick helped unravel one of the most damaging political scandals in Detroit history, pleaded guilty Monday to felony obstruction charges, closing another chapter in the perjury-and-cover-up case that forced Kilpatrick from office.**

Beatty’s plea marks a dramatic fall for one of City Hall’s most powerful insiders and a central figure in the scandal that consumed Detroit government for much of 2008. Her admission came after months of legal pressure stemming from testimony she and Kilpatrick gave in a whistle-blower lawsuit brought by former police officials who said they were punished for probing allegations tied to the mayor’s conduct and his security detail.

At the heart of the case were explosive text messages first reported by the **Detroit Free Press**, which contradicted sworn testimony from both Kilpatrick and Beatty. The messages showed the two had carried on a romantic relationship despite denying it under oath, and they suggested a coordinated effort to manage fallout from internal police investigations and the firing of officers who claimed retaliation.

The revelations triggered criminal charges, a political crisis at City Hall, and eventually extraordinary removal proceedings initiated by **Gov. Jennifer Granholm**, who convened hearings to determine whether Kilpatrick should be ousted from office for misconduct. Those hearings became a constitutional and political spectacle, putting the sitting mayor’s future in the hands of the governor even as prosecutors pursued criminal charges in Wayne County.

Kilpatrick ultimately resigned in September 2008 as part of a plea agreement, admitting to obstruction of justice and no contest to an assault-related charge. Beatty’s guilty plea now solidifies the prosecution’s case that the original civil trial was corrupted by false testimony and efforts to conceal the truth.

## Plea follows months of scandal

Beatty, once viewed as one of Kilpatrick’s closest advisers and a key force in his administration, admitted responsibility in connection with false statements and the handling of evidence tied to the whistle-blower litigation. Prosecutors said her actions helped obstruct the civil proceedings in which former police officials accused the mayor’s office of retaliation.

The whistle-blower lawsuit was filed by former Detroit police officials, including **Gary Brown**, a deputy police chief who said he was fired after investigating allegations involving Kilpatrick’s security unit. The case became politically explosive because it intersected with claims that the mayor’s office sought to conceal information about Kilpatrick’s personal conduct and the operations of his protection detail.

A jury awarded millions of dollars to the former officers in 2007. The city later reached an even larger settlement, but the matter did not end there. Questions soon emerged about whether the settlement was designed in part to keep damaging text messages from becoming public.

## Free Press texts changed everything

The scandal widened dramatically when the **Detroit Free Press** published excerpts from text messages between Kilpatrick and Beatty. The messages, sent on city-issued devices, revealed a personal relationship between the mayor and his chief of staff and appeared to contradict testimony they had given during the whistle-blower trial.

The texts included affectionate and sexually suggestive exchanges, but their legal significance went beyond the affair. They undercut sworn denials and raised questions about whether city officials had misled the court, jurors, and the public.

The Free Press report transformed what had been a civil employment dispute into a full-blown criminal and governmental crisis. Wayne County Prosecutor **Kym Worthy** brought perjury, obstruction, and misconduct charges against Kilpatrick and Beatty, accusing them of lying under oath and engaging in a cover-up.

## Granholm hearings intensified pressure

As the scandal deepened, Governor Granholm took the rare step of opening removal hearings against Kilpatrick. The proceedings examined whether the mayor had committed official misconduct and whether he should be removed from office before his term expired.

The hearings were unprecedented in modern Detroit politics and added enormous pressure on Kilpatrick, whose administration was already paralyzed by the criminal case, public outrage, and City Council demands for accountability. Granholm’s involvement underscored the seriousness of the crisis: the state’s top elected official was considering removing the elected mayor of Michigan’s largest city.

The hearings were ultimately overtaken by Kilpatrick’s plea deal and resignation. But they remain a defining moment in the scandal, demonstrating how the legal fallout from the text messages had escalated into a direct challenge to mayoral power.

## Aftermath for Detroit

Beatty’s guilty plea is another major turning point in a scandal that damaged public trust, cost taxpayers millions, and reshaped Detroit politics. The case exposed deep dysfunction inside City Hall and raised enduring questions about transparency, executive power, and the misuse of public resources.

Kilpatrick’s resignation elevated City Council President **Kenneth Cockrel Jr.** to the mayor’s office on an interim basis, beginning a period of political transition in a city already facing severe financial and social challenges.

For Beatty, the plea represents a public acknowledgment of wrongdoing after months of maintaining her defense. For Detroit residents, it is another reminder of how private misconduct, public deception, and institutional retaliation converged into one of the most consequential scandals in the city’s modern history.
